(p-220) Surah al-Qari'ah: its central theme

Clarifying the Day of Judgment (yawm al-din) by depicting the successive states of its beginning and its end, and dividing people in it into the saved and the lost. Its name, al-Qari'ah, is evident in this. "In the name of Allah" (bism Allah), the King, the Most High, "al-Rahman" (the Most Merciful), whose blessing of bringing into existence and clarifying has encompassed all creation; "al-Rahim" (the Especially Merciful), who singled out the people of His party with success in what is required and pleasing to Him.

* *

When He concluded Surat al-'Adiyat with the resurrection, He mentioned its blast, saying: ﴿The Striking Calamity﴾. That is, the Blast or the Resurrection. It was named so because it strikes the ears of people and pounds them with a severe, [great] pounding that disturbs them with terror, and the dense bodies with splitting and cleaving, and the fixed things with scattering.

Since it surpasses description in the greatness of its matter and the majesty of its dominion, he expressed this and increased its magnitude by naming it explicitly (bi'l-ilham wal-izhar) in the place where a pronoun would be expected (fi mawdi' al-idmar), indicating by the interrogative (bil-istifham) that it is something worthy of being asked about, in the manner of wonder and great esteem, so he said: ﴿What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ And he emphasized its magnitude [informing -] (p-221) that [whatever] comes to your mind of its greatness, it is greater than that, so he said:

When the listener has directed all his thought to grasping its circumstances, he says, with the following as its implied sense: it will occur, ﴿on the day when it occurs﴾, that is, an occurrence as if it were innate, ﴿the people﴾, that is, those whose condition is (p-222) confusion, despite their great numbers, the differences in their essences, conditions, ranks and measures, and their dispersal after the graves are overturned and what is in the breasts is brought forth, ﴿like moths﴾, that is, young locusts, because they spread out and hurl themselves into the fire. Or it is another kind of flying creature, without blood, which falls into the fire, and it is neither a gnat nor a fly. Hamzah al-Karmani said: He likened them to moths that fly from here and from there and do not travel in one direction, and they are insects that the lamp attracts. Others said: The aspect of likeness is the multitude, the dispersal, the weakness and the abjectness, and their flying toward the caller from every side, as moths fly, and the great number that hurl themselves into the fire, and some of them riding over others and surging over one another from the intensity of the terror, as God the Exalted said: ﴿as if they were scattered locusts﴾ [al-Qamar: 7]. ﴿scattered﴾, that is, spread out and dispersed.

When the mountains are at their most solid, the dread is greatest in the report of what will be done to them, so He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the mountains will be like wool(al-'ihn)﴾, [meaning] in the state they are in of firmness and solidity, and that they are firm rocks, ﴿like wool (al-'ihn)﴾, that is, dyed wool, because they are multicolored, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among the mountains are streaks, white and red﴾ [Fatir: 27], that is, and other than that. ﴿Fluffed(al-manfush)﴾, that is, carded, its parts scattered apart, not matted together with one another, (p-223) so you see them thereby flying about in the air like scattered dust, until the earth as a whole becomes level, with no crookedness in it and no elevation.

Since the Day is described according to what takes place in it, he consequently says, detailing it for them: ﴿As for him whose scales are heavy﴾, i.e., with weightiness. Since the things weighed are very numerous in kind, he used the plural for the scale in regard to them, saying: ﴿his scales﴾, i.e., the measures of the kinds of his good deeds, through following [the truth], because it is heavy in this world, and avoiding falsehood. The things weighed are the deeds themselves, embodied, and their records.

﴿So he﴾, because his good deeds outweigh (his bad ones), ﴿will be in a pleasant life﴾, meaning a life in which he moves about freely. Perhaps he attached the *hā'* (الهاء, the feminine ending that marks a single unit), and the intended meaning is "living," so that it is understood that it is in one state, in purity and pleasure, and not of varied conditions like the life of this world, ﴿well-pleasing﴾, meaning possessing contentment, or pleasing [because his mother -] a lofty garden.

﴿And as for one whose scales are light﴾ — i.e., whose scales ﴿are light﴾ (ṭāshat, that is, they went up and did not weigh down), ﴿his scales﴾ — meaning that his bad deeds outweigh his good, or he has no good deed at all, because he followed falsehood and it was light (weightless) to him in the world.

﴿Then his mother﴾ means the one who shelters him and gathers him to herself. The earth is likewise called *umm* (mother) because it is intended for that purpose, and a person settles into it as he settles into his mother, and so too a dwelling-place (*maskan*). The phrase conveys that he was created from her, and that the nature of Satan overcame him because the fiery element is the greater part of his constituents. It magnifies her by indefiniteness and by describing her with a term that marks her as having no floor (*qarar*): ﴿an abyss﴾, that is, a fire that descends, extremely low, so that he is such that he never ceases to plunge down into it, while he is in a displeasing life. This verse is an instance of *ihtibak* (the rhetorical device of mutual omission, in which each of two parts is left implicit and the other supplies its meaning). It mentions the life first as evidence for its omission later, and it mentions the mother second as evidence for her omission earlier. (p-224)

Since it is something whose description falls short because of the enormity of its terrors and the severity of its quaking, He gathered the matter concerning it and said, denying that any created being could know its description: ﴿And what will make you know what it is?﴾ That is, what could inform you of it, however hard you strain yourself? ﴿What is it?﴾ That is, al-Hawiyah (the Abyss), because no one has witnessed anything like it to measure it by. The heh of pause (haa' al-sakt) indicates that mentioning it is something that distresses the heart, so that one cannot go on speaking freely; or [alternatively] that it is something that befits the listener to have his hearing struck by this question about it, so that he falls silent in order to hear and understand the answer, in the utmost silence, and listens with the utmost attention.

When He had made it terrifying by what He mentioned, He followed it with what humans can grasp of its description, so He said: ﴿A blazing Fire﴾ — meaning its heat has reached its utmost. This is what you know of it among yourselves; as for its details, that is a matter only Allah Almighty knows. And this is the culmination of the Calamity (al-qari'ah), so the coherence of the first with the last is very clear and evident — and Allah knows best.
